title: Design UPI (Unified Payments Interface)
tagline: Move money between any two banks in seconds, without ever losing, duplicating or inventing a rupee.

statement.prompt: Design a **real-time payment system** like UPI. A person pays another person or a shop from their bank account to the other's, using only a virtual address or a QR code.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. The interviewer cares about **correctness and failure handling** more than boxes.
Many apps (PSPs) and many banks connect through a central **switch**.
Think about paying for tea by scanning a QR code.
given: Peak traffic is about **3 times** the average.
Each transaction writes about **2 ledger entries of 200 bytes**.
A payment should complete within a **few seconds**.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are idempotency, consistency across two banks, handling timeouts, and an auditable ledger.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: Routing between banks via a switch
great: Makes the **transaction id an idempotency key** at every hop.
Uses a **saga with reversals**, not a cross-bank transaction.
Treats a **timeout as unknown**, not as failure.
Keeps an **append-only double-entry ledger** and reconciliation.

concepts.def: Virtual payment address such as name@bank, so you do not share account numbers.
Payment service provider: the app and bank behind the app that connects users to the switch.
The central system that routes requests between banks and records results.
A series of local steps with compensating actions to undo them, used instead of a distributed transaction.
A unique id that makes repeating a request safe.
Comparing two systems' records to find and fix differences.
Every transfer records equal debit and credit entries, so the books always balance.

numbers: 15B per month = about **500M a day** = **5,800/s** average, **17,000/s** peak
Ledger: 500M x 2 x 200 B = **200 GB a day**, about **73 TB a year**
Availability target: **99.99%** is under **53 minutes** of downtime a year

takeaways: The **transaction id is the idempotency key** at every hop, so retries never double-charge.
Use a **saga: debit first, then credit, with compensating reversal**.
A **timeout is unknown**: show pending and reconcile with the same id.
Record money in an **append-only double-entry ledger**; fix errors with new entries.

steps.title: What must UPI do?
steps.hint: Money in, money out, and when it goes wrong.
steps.explain: Core: **pay, collect, status, balance, reversal.** Always add 'reversal': it signals you understand failure.

notes: Core: pay by VPA/QR, collect request, status check, balance, reversal

options.text: Check account balance
options.why: Common companion feature.

options.text: Check the status of a payment
options.why: People retry when unsure. Status must be reliable.

options.text: Pay another person or merchant using a virtual address (VPA), QR code or phone number
options.why: The headline feature.

options.text: Refunds and reversals when something fails
options.why: Money must never vanish.

options.text: Loan origination and credit scoring
options.why: A different product.

options.text: Request money (collect) and approve it
options.why: The other direction of the same flow.

steps.title: Qualities
steps.prompt: Rank what matters most for a payment rail.
steps.hint: What is worse: a slow payment or a duplicate one?
steps.explain: **Correctness before speed.** A slow payment annoys; a wrong one causes real loss.

notes: Qualities: correct (exactly-once effect), highly available, a few seconds latency, secure, auditable

options.text: High availability: people pay for groceries, not in a maintenance window
options.why: Downtime is visible to millions.

options.text: Low latency: finish within a few seconds
options.why: A person is standing at a counter.

options.text: Eventual consistency of balances is fine
options.why: A balance that is wrong for hours is not acceptable.

options.text: Auditability and reconciliation with banks
options.why: Regulators and banks both demand it.

options.text: Correctness: no double debit, no lost money, every rupee traceable
options.why: The number one requirement.

options.text: Security: encrypted PIN, device binding, fraud checks
options.why: Money attracts attackers.

steps.title: How many transactions per second?
steps.prompt: UPI handles about **15 billion** transactions a month. Peak is **3 times** the average. What is the **peak transactions per second**?
steps.hint: Month to day to second, then multiply for peak.
steps.explain: Roughly **6,000 average, 17,000 at peak**. Each payment touches several systems, so the switch and banks do many times that in internal calls. Design every shared component to scale horizontally.

steps.title: Ledger storage
steps.prompt: Each transaction creates about **2 ledger entries** of **200 bytes** each. How many **TB** of ledger is written per year at **500 million** transactions a day?
steps.explain: About **73 TB of ledger a year**, append-only. That is very manageable with partitioning by time and account, and cheap archive tiers for old data. Reads of recent data dominate.

notes: Storage: ~73 TB of ledger per year, append-only

work: 200 GB x 365 = 73,000 GB = about **73 TB a year**
Plus indexes and replicas: several times more

steps.title: Never charge twice
steps.prompt: The payer's phone loses signal after tapping Pay and the app retries. How do you guarantee only one debit?
steps.hint: How can the server recognise 'this is the same request'?
steps.explain: The **transaction id is the idempotency key**, generated by the client before the first attempt and kept for the retries.

notes: Idempotency: client-generated unique transaction id stored with its result at every hop

steps.pitfall: Retrying a debit with a new id.
steps.followup: Where is the id stored, and for how long?

options.text: Retry until the server answers
options.why: Without an id, each retry could debit again.

options.text: Let the bank detect duplicates by amount and time
options.why: Two genuine identical payments (tea twice) would be blocked.

options.text: Every payment has a unique transaction id; the switch and banks store it with the result and return the stored result on a repeat
options.why: Idempotency key: same id means same outcome.

options.text: Disable retries entirely
options.why: Networks fail; users would be stuck in doubt.

steps.title: Recording money
steps.prompt: How do you record the movement of money inside a ledger?
steps.explain: **Never edit history, add to it.** Mistakes are fixed with reversing entries. Balance = sum of entries (cached in a balance table for speed).

notes: Ledger: double-entry, append-only; mistakes fixed by reversal entries

options.text: Update a `balance` column in place and keep no history
options.why: No audit trail and lost-update bugs.

options.text: Store only the final balances at day end
options.why: Cannot explain what happened in between.

options.text: A **double-entry, append-only ledger**: each transfer adds a debit and a credit that sum to zero; balances are derived
options.why: Auditable, immutable, easy to reconcile.

options.text: Edit past entries when mistakes are found
options.why: Correct with a new reversing entry instead.

steps.title: A successful payment
steps.prompt: Order the main steps of a UPI payment.
steps.hint: Authorise, route, debit, credit, tell everyone.
steps.explain: **Debit then credit**, with the switch coordinating and recording. Fast path: no human steps, no batch jobs.

notes: Flow: PIN on device -> PSP -> switch resolves VPA -> debit payer bank -> credit payee bank -> record -> notify

items.text: The payer enters the amount and PIN; the PIN is encrypted on the device
items.why: Only the payer's bank can read it.

items.text: The app sends the request with a new transaction id to its PSP, which forwards it to the switch
The switch resolves the payee's VPA to a bank
The switch asks the payer bank to debit; then asks the payee bank to credit
items.why: Debit first: never credit money that has not left.

items.text: The switch records the result and both apps are notified

steps.title: Two banks, one payment
steps.prompt: Debit happens at Bank A, credit at Bank B. There is no single database spanning both. How do you keep the money consistent?
steps.hint: You cannot lock two companies' databases together.
steps.explain: **Saga + compensation.** Money is never created: debit before credit, and always have a reversal path.

notes: Consistency: saga (debit then credit) with compensating reversals; no distributed transaction across banks

steps.followup: What if the reversal itself fails?

options.text: Credit first, debit later
options.why: If the debit fails, money has been created.

options.text: Ignore failures and fix by hand
options.why: Millions of payments a day.

options.text: A **saga**: debit, then credit; if the credit fails, run a compensating **reversal** of the debit
options.why: Each step is local and atomic; failures are undone by a new step.

options.text: A distributed two-phase commit between all banks
options.why: Different organisations and systems, and it blocks when a participant is slow.

steps.title: The credit call timed out
steps.prompt: The switch asked the payee bank to credit and got no answer. What is the right action?
steps.hint: Do you know what happened on the other side?
steps.explain: **Timeout means unknown.** Resolve it with the same transaction id (idempotent enquiry or retry) and show the user 'pending' honestly.

notes: Timeouts mean unknown: status enquiry/reconciliation with the same id; show 'pending'

steps.pitfall: Treating a timeout as a failure.

options.text: Treat it as failed and reverse the debit immediately
options.why: The credit may have succeeded. The payee gets paid and the payer is refunded: money was created.

options.text: Mark the payment **pending**, and run status enquiry / reconciliation until the bank gives a definite answer, then complete or reverse
options.why: A timeout is not a failure; it is 'unknown'.

options.text: Retry the credit with a new id
options.why: May credit twice.

options.text: Tell the user it succeeded
options.why: A lie that may need correcting.

steps.title: Fraud and limits
steps.prompt: Which controls protect users and the network?
steps.hint: Who, how much, how unusual, what secret.
steps.explain: Layer controls: **identity (device), amount (limits), behaviour (risk score), secret (PIN)**.

notes: Fraud: device binding, limits, real-time risk scoring, PIN only readable by the bank

options.text: A PIN that only the bank can decrypt
options.why: Apps and the switch never see it.

options.text: Real-time risk scoring (velocity, new payee, odd hours)
options.why: Stops suspicious payments before debit.

options.text: Device binding and SIM verification at registration
options.why: Ties the account to a device.

options.text: Disable all limits for convenience
options.why: Invites fraud.

options.text: Per-transaction and daily limits
options.why: Caps losses from compromised accounts.

steps.title: Scale and availability
steps.prompt: Which choices help the rail stay up and fast?
steps.hint: Parallel across accounts, serial within one.
steps.explain: Keep the **critical path small** (verify, debit, credit, record) and put everything else on queues. Isolate slow banks.

notes: Scale/HA: shard by account, active-active sites, queues for non-critical work, per-bank circuit breakers

options.text: Partition ledgers and state by account id so work spreads across nodes
options.why: Single-account updates stay serialised, different accounts run in parallel.

options.text: Circuit breakers and a 'bank slow' mode that shows pending instead of timing out hard
options.why: One slow bank must not stop the rest.

options.text: A single database for the entire country
options.why: One machine, one failure.

options.text: Queues for notifications and non-critical work
options.why: Keep the critical path short.

options.text: Active-active data centres with replicated state
options.why: Survives a site loss.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what consistency model did you choose, and why?
steps.hint: Where is strong consistency a must, where is it unrealistic?
steps.explain: In payments, finish with: **"We never guess; we reconcile."**

notes: Trade-offs: ACID inside banks; saga + reconciliation across; pending states; operational cost

steps.model: Inside each bank's ledger I need **strong consistency** (ACID) because balances must be exact. Across banks I use a **saga with reversals and reconciliation**, so the end-to-end flow is **eventually consistent**, and a payment may show **pending** briefly. I accept this because a global distributed transaction across organisations would hurt availability and is not practical. The cost is operational: reconciliation jobs, reversal flows, and clear user messaging about pending states.
points: Pending state is an honest answer
